abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Fungi are increasingly recognized to play diverse roles within honey bee hives, acting as pathogens, mutualists, and commensals. Pollen products, essential for hive nutrition, host significant fungal communities with potential protective and nutritional benefits. In this study, we profile the fungal communities and antifungal properties of three pollen products from healthy and stressed hives: fresh pollen collected by forager bees from local plants; stored pollen packed into the comb inside the hive; and bee bread, which is stored pollen following anaerobic fermentation used for bee and larval nutrition. Using amplicon sequencing, we found significant differences in fungal community composition, with hive health and sample type accounting for 8.8% and 19.3% of variation in beta diversity, respectively. Pollen and bee bread extracts had species-specific antimicrobial activity and inhibited the fungal hive pathogens Ascosphaera apis, Aspergillus flavus, and Aspergillus fumigatus, and the bacterial hive pathogen Paenibacillus larvae. Activity was positively correlated with phenolic and antioxidant content and was diminished in stressed hives. The plant source of pollen determined by amplicon sequencing differed in stressed hives, suggesting altered foraging behaviour. These findings illustrate the complex interplay between honey bees, fungal communities, and hive products, which should be considered in hive management and conservation.

This study investigates the fungal communities and antimicrobial properties of honey bee pollen products, revealing significant differences in composition and activity between samples taken from healthy hives and hives experiencing minor stress.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Honey bees engage in diverse relationships with microorganisms, ranging from beneficial to parasitic (Engel et al. 2016). While research in this area has predominantly focused on bee-associated bacteria, there is a growing acknowledgment of the significance of other microorganisms, particularly fungi. Traditionally perceived as saprotrophs, pathogens, or spoilage microbes, fungi associated with bees are increasingly recognized to include commensal and mutualistic species (Rutkowski et al. 2023). The mechanisms through which honey bees maintain the balance between beneficial and harmful fungi within the hive, however, remain poorly understood.

Honey bees produce a variety of products with functional properties that contribute to the overall functioning and health of the colony including honey, wax, and propolis (Viuda-Martos et al. 2008, Fernandes et al. 2022). Among these, pollen products hold nutritional significance as the primary source of protein for the hive as well as providing other essential nutrients including amino acids, lipids, vitamins, minerals, and various macro and microelements (Wright et al. 2018, El Ghouizi et al. 2023). Notably, these pollen products harbour a significant fungal community that may play a protective role against harmful and spoilage microbes (Anderson and Mott 2023) and a beneficial role in nutrition (Parish et al. 2020).

Pollen is collected from flowers by forager bees, where it is mixed with a small amount of salivary gland secretions and nectar before being placed into specialized ‘pollen baskets’ on the bee’s hind legs (Goodman 2003). Upon returning to the hive, the forager bees deposit these collected pollen pellets directly into wax comb storage cells, typically around the brood. The stored pollen is then processed by worker bees who add further glandular secretions including various enzymes, finally covering it with a thin layer of honey (Tautz 2008). This mixture undergoes anaerobic fermentation by Lactobacillus bacteria, a process which is thought to preserve the nutrients, forming a final product known as ‘bee bread’ that is then consumed by both mature bees and larvae (Anderson et al. 2014, Nicolson et al. 2018, Wright et al. 2018).

In addition to their nutritional importance, bee-collected pollen and bee bread also have antimicrobial properties. Various studies have reported inhibitory actions of pollen extracts against fungi (Özcan et al. 2004, Morais et al. 2011, Kacániová et al. 2012, Abdelsalam et al. 2018). However, the scope and specificity of this antifungal activity is not well understood, and comparisons between studies are complicated by the use of different extraction methods (Didaras et al. 2020). With honey bee colonies facing increasing stressors from climate change, pesticides, pests, and pathogens, we need a better understanding of their natural defence mechanisms and the role of hive products such as pollen and bee bread in maintaining the balance between beneficial and harmful fungi.

In a previous study, we investigated the relationship between hive health, bee-associated microbial communities, and the antimicrobial activity of honey in a set of samples taken from three healthy hives and three hives with signs of minor stress that were present in a single apiary. We found honey from the healthy hives exhibited significantly higher antimicrobial activity, correlating with increased phenolic and antioxidant content, while the stressed hives had a more diverse microbial population, suggesting a compromised ability to regulate microbial balance (Fernandes et al. 2023). In this study, we extend our investigation to bee-collected pollen and bee bread from the same hives during the same experimental period, with the aim of investigating the fungal diversity and antimicrobial activity in these pollen products, and how they may be affected by hive stress. This research contributes to a broader understanding of the complex relationships between honey bees and microbial communities within the hive environment.

sec.title: Sample collection
sec.p: Samples were collected from an apiary at Tocal Agricultural College Bee Research and Training Centre in Paterson, NSW. Samples collected were from the same hives and at the same time as in our prior study (Fernandes et al. 2023). Professional on-site apiary managers selected three healthy hives and three hives experiencing signs of stress including low bee populations, absent queens, poor brood patterns, and signs of chalkbrood (with full details in Supplementary Table S1). From each hive, pollen pellets were collected from pollen traps fitted to the hive entrance on the morning of sampling (collected pollen), and freshly packed pollen with a dry appearance (stored pollen) and fermented bee bread with a wet appearance (bee bread) were collected from cells in the brood frames (Table 1). Sampling was performed on 17th March 2022, with additional pollen trap samples collected after a 2-week interval on 31st March 2022. After transport, pollen samples were stored at –80°C until use.

sec.title: DNA extraction and amplicon sequencing
sec.p: Approximately 100 mg of pollen samples were transferred to tubes containing 500 mg of 2-mm glass beads in 500 µl of PBS. Samples were homogenized in a bead beater using three cycles of 30 s at 3000 r/m with 30 s rests between. DNA extractions were performed using DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kits (Qiagen) according to manufacturer’s instructions. DNA concentration was measured using the Qubit dsDNA BR Assay Kit (Invitrogen). PCR and gel electrophoresis were conducted to confirm the presence of amplifiable DNA in samples. DNA was sent to BGI Genomics, Hong Kong for ITS2 amplicon sequencing with the fITS7-ITS4 primer set using the DNBSEQ PE300 platform. Final sample numbers were n = 11 for collected pollen, n = 6 for stored pollen, and n = 6 for bee bread from all experimental hives combined. Raw sequence reads were processed in R v4.2.2 using the DADA2 pipeline to remove low-quality reads, eliminate chimeras, and generate amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). After processing, there was an average of 58 470 reads per test sample, while the H2O-only negative control failed to produce a DNA library indicating no contamination. Fungal taxonomy was assigned using the UNITE database release 27.10.2022. To assign plant taxonomy, remaining sequences unassigned beyond the Kingdom level were run through NCBI Nucleotide Blast optimized for highly similar sequences and assigned at Genus level. Alpha diversity, beta diversity, and taxonomic relative abundance were calculated and visualized using the phyloseq and ggplot2 R packages.

sec.title: Preparation of pollen ethanolic extracts
sec.p: Approximately 1 g of pollen was accurately weighed and transferred to a 15-ml centrifuge tube and 80% ethanol was added at a ratio of 1:10 (% w/v) pollen to solvent. Tubes were vortexed thoroughly until pollen dispersed, placed in a foil-lined container to protect samples from light, and set on a shaker at ~50 r/m for 14 days to facilitate extraction. After the extraction period, tubes were centrifuged to pellet the pollen, and the supernatant was passed through a 0.22-µm pore syringe filter. The remaining liquid was transferred to a preweighed wide-mouth sample jar and allowed to evaporate naturally in a fume hood overnight. Once evaporated, the sample jars were weighed subtracting their initial weight to determine the final weight of extracts. Extracts were resuspended at a concentration of 400 mg/ml in DMSO and stored at –80°C until use.

sec.title: Microorganisms and culture conditions
sec.p: Test microorganisms included eight yeast species (Candida albicans SC5314, Candida metapsilosis M1879, Candida parapsilosis ATCC22018, Candida tropicalis M230640, Cryptococcus deuterogattii R265, Cryptococcus neoformans H99, Kluyveromyces marxianus M1896, and Meyerozyma guillierondii AMMRL1830), eight mould species (Alternaria alternata ACC02, Ascosphaera apis TCI01 isolated from a case of chalkbrood, Aspergillus flavus ATCC204304, Aspergillus fumigatus ATCC204305, Aspergillus lentulus DTO341-G7, Fusarium oxysporum ACC06, Penicillium sp MCC01, and Mucor circinelloides 80–14–240–5007), and two bacteria species (Staphylococcus aureus ATCC29213 and Paenibacillus larvae EMAI02 isolated from a case of American Foulbrood). All organisms were maintained as glycerol stocks at –80°C. Yeast and mould species were grown on Sabouraud dextrose agar (10 g peptone, 40 g glucose, 15 g agar, and 1 l H2O) and incubated at 25 or 30°C for 24–72 h except A. apis, which was incubated for upto 3 weeks until good sporulation was obtained. Staphylococcus aureus was grown on nutrient agar (Oxoid) and incubated at 30°C for 24 h. Paenibacillus larvae was grown on MYPGP agar (120 g Mueller–Hinton broth (MHB), 15 g yeast extract, 3 g K2HPO4, 1 g sodium pyruvate, 15 g agar, 20 ml 10% glucose, and 1 l H2O) and incubated at 30°C for 48 h.

sec.title: Antimicrobial susceptibility testing by broth microdilution
sec.p: Antimicrobial susceptibility testing by broth microdilution in 96-well plates was performed in accordance with CLSI guidelines for aerobic bacteria, yeasts, and filamentous fungi with minor modifications. Briefly, inocula were prepared from colonies growing on agar plates to a final concentration of 0.5 × 103–2.5 × 103 CFU/ml for yeasts, 0.4 × 104–5 × 104 for moulds, and 2 × 105–8 × 105 for bacteria. Fungal cells were counted using a haemocytometer while bacterial cultures were adjusted to an absorbance of between 0.08–0.1 at 625 nm using a spectrophotometer. Assays used RPMI-1640 (Sigma-Aldrich) supplemented with 0.165 M MOPS and 2% d-glucose for all yeasts and moulds except Cryptococcus, which used yeast nutrient broth (Sigma-Aldrich) supplemented with 0.165 M MOPS and 0.5% d-glucose, MHB (Oxoid) supplemented with 20 mg Ca++/l and 10 mg Mg++/l for S. aureus, and MYPGP broth (10 g MHB, 15 g yeast extract, 3 g K2HPO4, 1 g sodium pyruvate, 20 ml 10% glucose, and 1 l H2O) for P. larvae. Pollen extracts were assayed at a concentration range of 2–4096 µg/ml with the final concentration of DMSO no more than 1%. Amphotericin B was included as a drug control for fungi and tetracycline as a drug control for bacteria. Plates were incubated without agitation at 35°C for 18 h (S. aureus), 24 h (Candida spp., K. marxianus, M. circinelloides, and M. guilliermondii), 48 h (A. alternata, Aspergillus spp., Cryptococcus spp., F. oxysporum, and Penicillium sp.) or 96 h (A. apis). The MIC was determined visually and defined as the lowest drug concentration at which no visible growth was evident. Three independent biological repeats were performed for each pollen sample.

sec.title: Phenolic and antioxidant assays
sec.p: Phenolic content was measured using the FBBB assay and antioxidant content was measured using the FRAP assay as described previously in (Fernandes et al. 2024). Briefly, for the FBBB assay, 200 µl aliquots of 8 µg/ml pollen samples were prepared in triplicate with 20 µl of 0.1% FBBB reagent added and pipetted up and down vigorously for 30 s followed by 20 µl of 5% NaOH with incubation in the dark for 45 min at RT. Absorbance was measured at 420 nm using a plate reader and gallic acid standards ranging from 0.06 to 0.18 mg/ml were used to generate a standard curve and calculate the phenolic content of pollen samples, expressed as mg of gallic acid equivalent per gram of pollen (mg GAE/g). For the FRAP assay, 20 µl aliquots of 8 µg/ml pollen samples were prepared in triplicate with 180 µl of freshly prepared FRAP reagent [1:1:10 (v/v/v) of 10 mM 2,4,6-Tris(2-pyridyl)-s-triazine in 40 mM HCl, 20 mM FeCl3, and 300 mM pH 3.6 acetate buffer; prewarmed to 37°C] added with incubation for 30 min at 37°C. Absorbance was measured at 594 nm using a plate reader and FeSO4 standards (freshly made and stored on ice) ranging from 200 to 1200 µM were used to calculate FRAP value, expressed as µmol Fe2+/g.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Whether data were normally distributed was determined using the Shapiro–Wilk normality test. Significant differences between groups for nonparametric data were determined using Mann–Whitney U tests for two groups, or Kruskal–Wallis H tests with post hoc Dunn’s tests for >2 groups. Differences in variance were assessed by F-tests. Associations between nonparametric or parametric and nonparametric variables were assessed using Spearman’s rank correlations. Amplicon data (ASVs) were rarefied to even sampling depth prior to the calculation of alpha diversity metrics and were subject to centred-log ratio transformation for beta-diversity measures. For alpha diversity, total ASV count (observed), and the Shannon and InvSimpson indices were calculated using the phyloseq R package. For beta diversity, Bray–Curtis dissimilarity matrices were calculated and NMDS was performed using the phyloseq R package. Permutational ANOVAs (ADONIS) and analysis of similarity (ANOSIM) were performed using the vegan R package. For comparisons of relative abundance, one-way ANOVAs with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction were used. Unless otherwise specified, two-tailed P-values were used for all tests, and P-values < .05 were considered significant. Error bars represent the mean +/− 95% standard error of measurement (SEM). Data were analysed and visualized using Excel (Microsoft), Prism 10 (GraphPad), and R v4.2.2 software.

sec.title: The fungal community in pollen products varies significantly with hive health
sec.p: Three types of pollen sample were used in this study and were termed collected pollen, stored pollen, and bee bread, with details of bee processing and the sampling methods outlined in Table 1. The fungal community of these pollen samples was assessed via ITS rRNA gene sequencing. Three measures of alpha diversity were used to compare pollen samples: Observed, which is the number of unique ASVs in the sample, the Shannon index which gives more weight to species richness, and the Inverse Simpson (InvSimpson) index, which gives more weight to species evenness (Fig. 1A). Considering all pollen sample types together, alpha diversity assessed by Shannon and InvSimpson was significantly greater in pollen from stressed hives than in that from healthy hives (P = .025 and P = .008, respectively). Shannon alpha diversity was more variable (P = .017) in pollen from healthy hives.

caption.p: Alpha and beta diversity of fungi in pollen provisions vary significantly with hive health status. (A) Fungal alpha diversity in collected pollen, stored pollen, and bee bread measured using total ASV count (observed), and the Shannon (species richness) and Inverse Simpson’s (species evenness) indices. Error bars show the mean and SEM, while circles show the values of individual samples. Significant differences between means (t-test) and variances (F-test) are shown on the graphs in blue and red, respectively. (B) Fungal beta diversity shown as nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) plots using Bray–Curtis dissimilarity matrices and grouped by pollen sample type (left plot) or hive health status (right plot) with the distance between points indicating their level of similarity. Ellipses show the 95% confidence interval of each sample type. R2 and P-values for ADONIS analysis that shows whether significant amounts of variation are explained by certain groupings, and ANOSIM analysis that shows whether samples are significantly more similar within than between groups, are shown in the box below.

sec.p: Multivariate analysis was next used to assess differences in fungal beta diversity between pollen sample types and between healthy and stressed hives. Nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS)-based Bray–Curtis dissimilarity matrices showed overlapping but distinct separation of samples according to sample type and hive health (Fig. 1B). ADONIS on the Bray–Curtis dissimilarities, which determines whether significant amounts of variation are explained by certain groupings, showed that overall, 19.3% of variation was significantly accounted for by sample type (P = .010) and 8.8% of variation was significantly accounted for by hive health (P = .039). ANOSIM analysis, which shows whether samples are significantly more similar within than between groups, further indicated that there was significantly greater variation between samples than within samples for sample type (R2 = 0.205; P = .009) but not for hive health. These results indicate that pollen sample type and hive health status are both significant drivers of variation in the fungal community of honey bee pollen products.

Figure 2(A)–(C) shows the relative abundance for fungal genera comprising ≥1% of the fungal community averaged across each pollen sample type. In collected pollen, the most abundant genus was Zygosaccharomyces (29.2%), followed by Nigrospora (8.7%) and Cladosporium (6.6%). In stored pollen, samples were dominated by Cladosporium (34.9%), with the next most abundant genera being Metschnikowia (10.1%) and Alternaria (7.1%). In bee bread, rather than a single dominant genus, there were five genera present at a similar abundance: Cladosporium (11.2%), Metschnikowia (9.9%), Moniliella (9.6%), Nigrospora (9.2%), and Starmerella (8.3%), with remaining genera being <3% each.

caption.p: Relative abundance of fungi varies among pollen provisions and with hive health status. Relative abundances of fungi in (A) collected pollen, (B) stored pollen, and (C) bee bread. Values shown are the mean across all samples of one type. Taxa with averaged relative abundance ≥1% are shown, while those <1% are grouped under ‘Other’. The total number of taxa identified was 160 for collected pollen, 127 for stored pollen, and 145 for bee bread.

sec.title: Plant origin of pollen products indicates varied hive foraging behaviour
sec.p: ITS sequences unassigned a taxonomy below the Kingdom level were subjected to NCBI Nucleotide Blast for potential plant DNA identification, with subsequent assignment of plant taxonomy at the genus level. The primer pair fITS7/ITS4 used in the current study, although designed to be fungal selective, is known to also amplify a diverse range of plant sequences (Ihrmark et al. 2012). Thus, while these data may not capture the full spectrum of plant DNA in the sample, they can indicate changes in relative abundance of amplifiable plant sequences between samples. NMDS based on Bray–Curtis dissimilarity matrices showed an overlapping but distinct grouping of samples according to hive health (Fig. 3A). ADONIS showed that 12.6% of variation was significantly accounted for by hive health (P = .040) with ANOSIM analysis further indicating that there was significantly greater variation between pollen samples from healthy and stressed hives than within these groups (R2 = 0.158, P = .031). Sample type had no significant explanatory power. Figure 3(B) shows the relative abundance of plant genera averaged across pollen samples for healthy hives and stressed hives. Healthy hive pollen had a significantly lower relative abundance of the genus Corymbia (q < .001) and a significantly higher relative abundance of the genus Ricinus (q < .001) than stressed hive pollen, suggesting differences in foraging behaviour (Fig. 3C).

caption.p: Plant diversity and abundance indicates differences in foraging behaviour between hives. (A) Plant beta diversity shown as NMDS plots using Bray–Curtis dissimilarity matrices and grouped by pollen sample type (left plot) or hive health status (right plot) with the distance between points representing the level of similarity between samples. Ellipses show the 95% confidence interval of each sample type. R2 and P-values for ADONIS analysis that shows whether significant amounts of variation are explained by certain groupings, and ANOSIM analysis that shows whether samples are significantly more similar within than between groups, are shown in the box below. (B) Relative abundances of plant DNA in pollen from healthy (left panel) and stressed (right panel) hives. Values shown are averaged across all samples of one type. Taxa with averaged relative abundance ≥1% are shown, while remaining taxa are grouped under ‘Other’. The total number of taxa identified was 34 for healthy hives and 35 for stressed hives. (C) Significant differences between the relative abundances of the genera Corymbia and Ricinus in all pollen samples in healthy and stressed hives calculated using one-way ANOVAs with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction. Columns represent the mean while diamonds show the values of individual samples. Error bars show SEM.

sec.title: Pollen extracts exhibit species-specific antimicrobial activity against hive pathogens
sec.p: The antifungal activity of ethanolic extracts of pollen samples from each hive across the three sample types was tested in order to determine whether pollen possesses antifungal properties, and if so, the breadth of this activity against diverse fungi and whether it aligns with hive health. A range of yeast and mould species that were found to be present in the pollen mycobiome was selected for testing. Individual values for each pollen extract are shown in Supplementary Table S1. Figure 4(A) and (B) compares the average activity of all pollen extracts from healthy versus stressed hives, with the geomean for each sample type shown in Table 2. Pollen extracts were found to have strongly species-specific antifungal activity, displaying activity against Cryptococcus deuterogattii (geomean 1515 µg/ml), Cryptococcus neoformans (geomean 614 µg/ml), Alternaria alternata (geomean 651 µg/ml), Ascosphaera apis (geomean 2310 µg/ml), Aspergillus flavus (geomean 1227 µg/ml), and Aspergillus fumigatus (geomean 1343 µg/ml) but not against Candida, Kluyveromyces, Meyerozyma, Aspergillus lentulus, Fusarium, Mucor, or Penicillium. As susceptible species included hive pathogens A. apis (causative agent of chalkbrood), A. flavus and A. fumigatus (causative agents of stonebrood), testing was extended to the bacterial hive pathogen Paenibacillus larvae (causative agent of American foulbrood; Fig. 4C). Pollen extracts were active against P. larvae (geomean 672 µg/ml), but not against nonhive pathogen Staphylococcus aureus.

caption.p: Pollen extracts have species-specific antifungal and antibacterial activity. The antimicrobial activity of all pollen extracts against selected (A) yeasts, (B) moulds, and (C) bacteria. Columns represent the geomean while diamonds show the values of individual samples. Error bars show SEM. Microbes were selected based on their presence in the pollen microbiome, with GP indicating the genus was present, and SP indicating the species was present. HP indicates a known hive pathogen. (D) Spearman correlation matrix showing how closely the antimicrobial activity of pollen samples aligns between different species. Each cell represents a pairwise comparison, with the correlation coefficient indicating the similarity in their susceptibility to the pollen samples. Points closer to 1 indicate high similarity, while points closer to 0 indicate low similarity. All correlations were positive, with the colour scalebar indicating the level of correlation. * = P ≤ .05, ** = P ≤ .01, *** = P ≤ .001.
Antimicrobial activity of pollen samples grouped by type and hive health status.

sec.p: Pollen from healthy hives was, on average, more active than that from stressed hives against every susceptible species, reaching statistical significance against A. alternata (P = .012), A. fumigatus (P = .010), and P. larvae (P = .045). A consistent pattern was observed when comparing pollen sample types, with collected pollen displaying the strongest activity, substantially lower activity in stored pollen, and generally intermediate activity in bee bread (Table 2). To assess whether the susceptibility profiles of certain microbes were significantly different from each other, rank correlations were performed (Fig. 4D). These were always positive but only reached statistical significance in 11/21 pairs suggesting some level of species-specific differences in susceptibility to certain samples. Notably, the hive pathogens A. apis and A. flavus showed the weakest correlations with other microbes. This suggests that these pathogens may exhibit unique resistance to certain compounds present in the samples, or alternatively that specific samples contain compounds to which A. apis and A. flavus are particularly susceptible.

sec.title: Phenolic and antioxidant content are linked to hive health and antimicrobial activity
sec.p: In our previous study on the same hives, we found phenolic and antioxidant content to be positively correlated with the antimicrobial activity of honey samples (Fernandes et al. 2023). To determine whether this extended to pollen samples, the phenolic and antioxidant content of pollen extracts were measured using fast blue BB (FBBB) and ferric-reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) assays, respectively (Fig. 5A and B). Phenolic content was significantly greater in pollen from healthy hives (P = .038) with an average of 72 mg GAE/g compared to that from stressed hives, with an average of 36 mg GAE/g. Antioxidant content was greater on average in the healthy hive pollen (49 µmol Fe2+/g) compared to the stressed hive pollen (44 µmol Fe2+/g), but this did not reach statistical significance. Significant correlations were found with antimicrobial activity and alpha diversity (Fig. 5C). Increased phenolic (r = −0.705; P = < .001) and antioxidant (r = −0.733; P < .001) content were significantly correlated with decreased average MIC (calculated as the geomean of MIC values for every susceptible microbe). Antioxidant content was additionally negatively correlated with InvSimpson alpha diversity of fungal and plant ASVs combined (r = −0.493; P = .046).

caption.p: Phenolic and antioxidant content of pollen extracts vary significantly with hive health status. (A) Phenolic and (B) antioxidant content of pollen extracts grouped by sample type and hive health status. Columns represent the mean while diamonds show the values of individual honey samples. Error bars show SEM. (C) Significant correlations between antimicrobial activity and phenolic content (left), antimicrobial activity and antioxidant content (middle), and alpha diversity (fungal + plant ASVs) and antioxidant content (right). Average MIC was calculated as the geomean of the MICs for all susceptible microbes. Lines of best fit and 95% confidence intervals, Spearman’s rho and P-values are shown.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In our previous study examining honey taken from three healthy hives and three hives suffering minor stress (e.g. low bee populations, absent queens, poor brood patterns, and signs of chalkbrood) from the same apiary, we established a connection between hive stress, reduced antimicrobial activity and altered chemical composition in honey, and deceased microbial diversity in the hive environment. We hypothesized that these compositional changes in honey might extend to other hive products and could partly result from distinct foraging behaviours between healthy and stressed hives. In the current study examining pollen products from the same hives taken during the same experimental period, we confirm a parallel decrease in the antimicrobial activity and phenolic content of pollen products from stressed hives and reaffirm the correlation between increased antioxidant content and reduced microbial diversity in bee bread across all hives. We additionally show evidence for a connection between hive health and foraging behaviour, with the diversity of plant ASVs in pollen samples significantly different between healthy and stressed hives. Overall, these results further support the notion that bee hive products play an important role in regulating microbial balance within the hive, which is perturbed in hives experiencing even minor stress.

The various pollen extracts had distinct species-specific antimicrobial activity across a diverse array of microbes. Looking at fungi, no activity was seen against Candida, Kluyveromyces, Meyerozyma, Fusarium, Mucor, and Penicillium. Members of these genera are reported to be prevalent in the fungal communities associated with bees or bee hives and likely play neutral or beneficial roles within the hive environment (Rutkowski et al. 2023). In contrast, pollen extracts demonstrated robust antifungal activity against A. apis, the causative agent of chalkbrood (Aronstein and Murray 2010), and within the Aspergillus genus, antifungal activity was found against A. flavus and A. fumigatus, causative agents of stonebrood (Becchimanzi and Nicoletti 2022), but not against the nonpathogen A. lentulus, revealing apparent specificity in antifungal action.

In addition to known hive pathogens, pollen extracts exhibited activity against A. alternata and Cryptococcus spp. Members of the Alternaria genus are plant pathogens (Thomma 2003), and studies have demonstrated the inhibitory effect of plant-derived compounds against these fungi (Carvalho et al. 2011, Lira-de León et al. 2014), suggesting that pollen-derived phytochemicals could be the source of the activity observed in the current study. Members of the genus Cryptococcus, however, are environmental saprotrophs and opportunistic pathogens of humans and are not known to be associated with plant diseases (May et al. 2016). The identification of C. neoformans in various insect-associated environments including bee colonies (Ergin et al. 2004), wasp nests (Gezuele et al. 1993), and insect frass (Kidd et al. 2002) has previously led to the hypothesis that it may be an insect-associated saprotroph or pathogen (Byrnes et al. 2011), though this remains unproven. The potent antifungal activity of pollen extracts against these organisms could therefore be bee-derived, and if so, this suggests that Cryptococcus spp. may have a negative effect on bee health.

For the two bacterial species tested, pollen extracts were active against P. larvae, the causative agent of American Foulbrood (Genersch 2010), but not against S. aureus. While Staphylococcus is not typically associated with bees or the hive environment, S. aureus is commonly utilized in honey antimicrobial testing and exhibits high susceptibility to honey. Our previous study investigating honey from the same hives found a significant correlation between the phenolic content of honey and antimicrobial activity against S. aureus (Fernandes et al. 2023). The absence of activity of the pollen extracts against S. aureus in the current study is therefore notable, given the strong correlation between phenolic content and pollen extract activity for other bacterial and fungal species. The most likely explanation for this divergence is that phenolic compounds in honey originate primarily from nectar rather than pollen. Although nectar and pollen generally contain distinct compositions, there may be some overlap in phenolic compounds when sourced from the same plant (Cook et al. 2013, Palmer-Young et al. 2019). A recent study investigating honey bee foraging choices found that while honey bees used mostly the same plants for both nectar and pollen, fewer plant genera and higher selectivity was used for pollen sources (Leponiemi et al. 2023). This is also influenced by whether a particular plant species provides both pollen and nectar for bees. Therefore, another plausible explanation for our findings could be divergence or increased selectivity in the pollen plant sources foraged during the study period compared to nectar.

The antimicrobial activity of pollen extracts varied with sample type. We found activity to be the highest in collected pollen, significantly lower in stored pollen, and intermediate in bee bread. These results diverge from those of a previous study that compared the ability of pollen collected from flowers, pollen collected from honey bee pollen baskets, and bee bread to inhibit P. larvae, and found a consistent increase in activity with further bee-processing (Crailsheim and Riessberger-Galle 2001). One likely source of discrepancy in these results is that it is challenging to accurately estimate the age of bee bread within the hive. Bees preferentially consume fresher bee bread within around 3–5 days of collection, with the rest consumed within a 2–3-week period (Roessink and van der Steen 2021) and may also feed on and replenish bee bread within a single cell (Didaras et al. 2020). In the current study, an increase in activity from stored pollen to bee bread was observed, and it is possible that the antimicrobial properties would have continued developing over time if stored for longer. The significant decrease in activity seen between collected and stored pollen was unexpected, though one possible explanation is the introduction of detoxifying enzymes through bee secretions, that have been shown to degrade toxic plant alkaloids (Haas et al. 2023).

The origin of antimicrobial activity in the pollen extracts may trace back to various sources. Plants are a rich source of phenolic and antimicrobial compounds, with many employed as natural defences against their own pathogens (Pratyusha 2022). Bees are attracted to pollen based on various factors such as colour, particle size, and lipid content (Pernal and Currie 2002, Hempel de Ibarra et al. 2014) and may even extend their selectivity to the presence of active secondary plant metabolites (Stevenson et al. 2017). Our observations of distinct foraging behaviour tied to hive health, coupled with the observation of heightened antimicrobial and phenolic content in pollen from healthy hives, supports this idea. The healthy hives had stronger populations and would therefore have a greater need for pollen collection, possibly collecting pollen from more diverse sources than stressed hives. However, the specificity of activity against hive pathogens suggests that bees may also introduce antimicrobial compounds. Bee secretions from various glands including hypopharyngeal, mandibular, venom, and wax glands are known to harbour compounds with antimicrobial properties (Cane et al. 1983, Vannette et al. 2015, Ratajczak et al. 2021), and these could be introduced to pollen upon collection and processing.

A third possible source of active compounds in pollen products is microbial metabolites. This idea is supported by our observation of differences in alpha diversity and relative abundance of specific fungi between healthy and stressed hives. The concept that fermentation by microbes improves the nutritional value of pollen by predigestion has been challenged, with studies finding no apparent nutrient conversion or increase in digestibility of pollen grains after their transformation to bee bread (Anderson et al. 2014, Nicolson et al. 2018). It has instead been proposed that microbes play a crucial role in the preservation of bee bread, potentially by producing compounds that inhibit the growth of pathogenic and spoilage microbes. Starmerella species, which we found to be more abundant in some bee bread samples from healthy hives, produce sophorolipids with antimicrobial properties thought to contribute to the preservation of bee products (Kurtzman et al. 2010, Hipólito et al. 2020, Rutkowski et al. 2023). A study using various Lactobacillus species has further shown that antimicrobial activity can develop and increase in pollen following fermentation (Di Cagno et al. 2019), with another study finding a significant increase in phenolic and antioxidant activity in collected pollen following lab-induced fermentation (Baltrusaityte et al. 2007).

Fungi can reach substantial density in bee bread (Anderson and Mott 2023), and their presence may enhance the nutritional benefits of bee bread compared to pollen. Recent studies have found that consumption of diets containing fungal spores increases the longevity of honey bee workers (Parish et al. 2020), that a species of stingless bee derives essential sterols from the consumption of Zygosaccharomyces sp. (Paludo et al. 2018), and that pollen microbes provide substantial nutrition to mason bees (Dharampal et al. 2019). Bee bread has been found to undergo fungal community succession over time, initially resembling fungal communities found in floral resources, followed by a decrease in abundance of flower-associated taxa and an increase in abundance of bee-associated taxa (Detry et al. 2020). This aligns with our findings of significant differences in the beta diversity of fungal communities between collected and stored pollen and bee bread. While the precise role of fungi in pollen products remains undetermined, the observed alterations in the fungal communities between healthy and stressed hives and the connection of this with antimicrobial activity and chemical composition suggests a functional importance that may be linked to the preservation and nutritional enhancement of bee products.

sec.title: Limitations and conclusions
sec.p: Our study explores the relationship between honey bee hive health and the fungal communities and antimicrobial properties of their pollen products. The observed variations in fungal diversity and antimicrobial potency in pollen products from healthy and stressed hives sheds light on the dynamic nature of hive ecosystems. However, several limitations should be acknowledged to contextualize our findings and guide future research. The sample size in our study was relatively small, which limits generalizing our results to larger hive populations. Our study focused on hives sourced from a single location, and does not address various hive-specific factors, such as geographic location, hive management practices, and the genetic diversity of bee populations. Finally, the methodology we employed has limitations, including that ethanolic extracts may not capture the full range of activity present in pollen samples, and that amplicon sequencing is affected by inherent amplification biases. Nonetheless, our findings emphasize the potential functional significance of pollen products in maintaining microbial balance in the hive and underscore the importance of understanding the relationships between hive health, hive products, and microbial communities for informing effective honey bee management and conservation strategies.
